transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2028-06-20 09:00 PT / 16:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Evan Ortiz (Redwood SE), Lina Park (Redwood SA); Ravi Menon (CTO, Arborlane), Sofia Alvarez (ML Eng), Greg Hsu (Platform Lead), Keisha Brown (Security), Tom Low (Product), Antoine (intern)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
- Arborlane is evaluating a vendor switch from OpenAI + vLLM in-house stack to Redwood (hosted or private). Primary drivers: cost predictability, reliability at scale, and compliance for regulated customers.
- Immediate asks: eval parity on current prompts, private VPC options, KMS/HSM integration, and a short perf pilot.
- Next: Redwood to run a parity eval + perf baseline; customer to share prompt set and failure examples.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — can you hear me okay?
[00:03] Ravi (Arborlane): Yep, loud and clear. Morning from SF.
[00:06] Sofia (Arborlane): good here. audio a little echoey, but fine.
[00:15] Maya: Great. Quick intros — I'm Maya, AE at Redwood. Evan's our systems SE, Lina does architecture. Over to you for quick intros?
[00:22] Ravi: I'm Ravi, CTO. Sofia leads the ML infra for our recommender product. Greg runs platform. Keisha is security and compliance. Tom manages product. Antoine is shadowing.
[00:31] Evan (Redwood SE): Nice to meet you all. We'll try to keep it practical — latency/cost/sample parity, and the network/security questions up front.

[02:00] Tom (Product): To set context: we run a hybrid approach today. Frontend calls OpenAI via API for most generation, but we also run vLLM locally for lower cost bursts and some private PII workloads. We're investigating consolidating to a single provider or a predictable dedicated environment.
[02:18] Maya: Helpful. What are the top success criteria for a migration?
[02:22] Ravi: Three things — 1) parity on our prompt outputs (must match our existing quality thresholds), 2) predictable per-token economics and capacity for 99.9pct uptime, 3) compliance — SOC2 + encrypted keys, and support for our KMS (we use AWS KMS + a hardware module for some customers).
[02:45] Keisha (Security): Also SSO via SAML, granular RBAC, audit logs retention for 12 months, and egress filtering for the Private run.

[05:10] Evan: Good, all standard. Quick question on the vLLM pieces — are you running a custom TGI/vLLM pipeline with model sharding or standard single-host instances?
[05:20] Sofia: It's a mix — we use vLLM on prem for most 13B/30B models and TGI for the fine-tuned bits. There's a wrapper that does batching and prefix caching — we call it our kv-cache shim, sometimes the memstore gets weird under pressure.
[05:38] Evan: Understood, that explains the caching mentions. On Redwood we have prefix/KV caching primitives and can map your current cache behavior to our runtime — sometimes tokenization or subtle sampling seeds differ, so we'll need eval parity tests.

[07:00] Ravi: On costs — our CFO is worried that hosted APIs ballooned last year, and the in-house vLLM saved money but had ops overhead. We're evaluating dedicated reserved capacity vs private VPC/deploy. Thoughts?
[07:18] Lina (Redwood SA): Tradeoff is predictability vs ops burden. Hosted gives fastest time-to-value, dedicated reserves GPU pools for predictable throughput and cost curve, while Private gives you the same control but with customer networking and keys. If you want KMS+HSM and egress controls, Private is usually the default for regulated flows.
[07:40] Greg: We also need autoscaling to handle traffic spikes from marketing campaigns — can Redwood burst beyond reserved?
[07:48] Maya: Yes, Dedicated supports configured burst capacity. We can set policies so you keep baseline reserved and only pay incremental when bursting.

[09:15] Sofia: Technical parity question — our prompts rely on streaming function-calling and a custom few-shot template. Will Redwood preserve request-level ordering and function call payloads?
[09:27] Evan: We support streaming and function/tool calling. Implementation detail: function-calling signatures are mapping-based; sometimes field names are normalized. We'll run your prompt set through our streaming path and check structural fidelity. A few customers saw minor whitespace/tokenization diffs with certain tokenizers.
[09:45] Tom: What about model variants? We use a fine-tuned 13B and a 70B for long context.
[09:52] Lina: You can pin model versions; we also have quantized variants for cost. We'll map your fine-tuned model to a compatible runtime image and validate behavioral parity.

[12:00] Keisha: About encryption — we need BYOK/HSM support and audit logs. Do you support customer-managed keys and do you expose key rotation events in logs?
[12:12] Maya: We integrate with KMS providers and HSM via our Private offering. Audit logs include key ops metadata; we'll share the security pack.
[12:24] Keisha: And data retention, can you set retention rules per workspace?
[12:29] Lina: Yes, retention and redaction policies are configurable for Private and Dedicated; hosted has defaults but we can discuss enterprise retention add-ons.

[15:00] Ravi: Performance baseline — we see p95 token latency of ~120ms on our tuned 13B for 512-token responses today. Can Redwood match that?
[15:10] Evan: We should be able to. Latency depends on batching, KV cache hits, and kernel selection. We'll need a perf pilot with your exact workload (batch distribution, sequence length) to guarantee p95. For initial estimates we can share our published benchmarks but recommend running the 1-week pilot.
[15:35] Sofia: Our current setup uses a lot of prefix reuse which keeps costs down. How does Redwood's caching work? Any gotchas with conversational state?
[15:47] Lina: We do automatic prefix/KV caching; the core difference is that we manage eviction policies centrally, and when you move to Dedicated/Private you can tune TTLs. If you have keyed reuse semantics, we'll map those to our KV layer. One gotcha: different tokenizers can change cache hit rates, so check parity.

[18:00] Tom: On the migration timeline, leadership wants a plan: pilot in July, then production by Q4 if pilot looks good. Is that realistic?
[18:12] Maya: Totally reasonable. Typical timeline: 1-2 weeks to set up eval cluster and run parity, 1 week perf/scale pilot, then engagement for Dedicated contract/Private onboarding — so Q4 is feasible.

[20:30] Ravi: A couple of pain points — our existing infra has a custom auth proxy and we do token masking before sending to OpenAI. We'd want to keep that pattern. Can Redwood accept proxied connections and preserve headers?
[20:45] Evan: Yes, our API supports upstream proxies and custom headers. For Private deployments we can put the control plane behind your SAML and RBAC. We'll want an architecture doc from Greg to validate network paths.

[24:00] Sofia: About model tooling — we use TGI for some finetune/special ops. Does Redwood support loading TGI checkpoints, or are there conversion steps?
[24:15] Lina: We can ingest standard model formats; for TGI there are sometimes nuances in the config and custom layers. We often do a compatibility pass where our model team converts and validates, but if you're shipping a custom TGI artifact we'll need the config/weights and a small runbook.

[26:30] Keisha: Legal/procurement question: we need a Data Processing Addendum and mention of subprocessor list — can you provide that before pilot?
[26:38] Maya: Yes, we'll include DPA, subprocessor list, and standard SLA language. We'll flag any dedicated/private-specific terms.

[29:00] Antoine (intern, low audio): quick — are you... are you able to run inference on-prem too?
[29:06] Evan: Short answer: yes, Private can be deployed on-prem with the customer-managed control plane, subject to airgap constraints. We've done a few air-gapped installs; they require more time for onboarding and security review.

[32:10] Ravi: Pricing — show me a scenario where Redwood Dedicated beats our vLLM in-house economics.
[32:22] Lina: The math depends on utilization and amortization of ops. If your utilization is high and you can handle ops, vLLM can be cheaper raw. But Dedicated reduces ops headcount, provides predictable reserved pricing, and includes autoscaling fallback for spikes. We'll run a unit-cost model with your usage numbers during the eval.

[35:00] Sofia: We have a tricky failure case: under heavy load we see weird token duplication from our TGI path. Will Redwood reproduce or fix that?
[35:12] Evan: We'll run your failure cases during parity tests — if we reproduce it, our runtime team will dig into sampling and seeding differences. Sometimes duplication comes from batching boundaries or from custom temperature scheduling. We'll add that to the test plan.

[38:45] Greg: Networking constraints for Private — we need to ensure egress to certain partners is blocked and that the instances are in our VPC. Can you accommodate strict egress rules and private endpoints?
[38:55] Lina: Yes, Private supports customer VPC and egress control. We usually provide a connectivity diagram and work with your networking to handle peering, firewalls, and NAT rules.

[41:00] Tom: Who will be the SE lead if we start the pilot?
[41:05] Maya: Evan will lead the SE work, Lina will help the architecture bits, and I'll coordinate commercial.

[43:30] Ravi: We may also want to retain some on-prem vLLM for ultra-sensitive datasets even after migration. Can Redwood support hybrid routing?
[43:40] Lina: Absolutely. We support smart routing policies: route by workload (latency vs cost), and fallback to on-prem variant when necessary. Many customers keep a private fallback for sensitive PII flows.

[46:15] Keisha: A final security question — do you provide signed attestations for model weights and a hash for integrity checks?
[46:25] Evan: We can provide checksums and attestations for the server-side images we deploy; for customer-provided weights we recommend storing them in your KMS/backed artifact store and we'll validate checksums before loading.

[49:00] Maya: Ok, to keep momentum, here's what we'll do next: Evan will provision an eval cluster, Sofia will send the prompt suite, Greg will give the network doc, Maya will send pricing and security pack. Any additions?
[49:12] Ravi: Add the parity failure cases and list of top 20 prompts.
[49:20] Sofia: I'll also include a short script to reproduce the token-dup bug.

[51:00] Maya: Great — I'd like to propose a follow-up checkpoint after the first parity run, maybe a check-in mid next week. Does that work for you?
[51:08] Ravi: Yep, mid next week is good.

[54:30] Tom: One more — is there a performance SLA for Dedicated?
[54:38] Lina: We offer SLA-backed uptime and latency targets at the Dedicated tier; exact numbers depend on contract and reserved capacity. We'll include SLA language in the materials.

[56:10] Maya: Thanks everyone. I'll send a recap and the artifacts we discussed. Appreciate the time.
[56:18] Greg: Thanks.
[56:20] Keisha: Thanks all.
[56:28] Sofia: bye.
[56:30] End of recording.

Attachments referenced: Hosted vs Dedicated pricing sheet (link), Redwood Security Pack (link), Eval runbook (link), Arborlane prompt suite (to be shared by customer).
